title: Structured Programming
overview: Topic 9.1 showed how decomposition turns a problem into modules; this topic is about writing those modules in Cambridge pseudocode. Paper 2 expects a procedure written as PROCEDURE … ENDPROCEDURE and run with CALL, taking none, one or several parameters; a function written as FUNCTION … RETURNS <type> … ENDFUNCTION whose RETURN value takes the place of the call inside an expression; and parameters marked BYVAL or BYREF, with a trace showing whether the caller's variable has changed after the call. Candidates must also explain when a procedure or a function is the right choice, use the words header, interface, parameter, argument and return value accurately, and write pseudocode that does not waste work. Marks are lost for putting CALL in front of a function, for a function with no RETURN on some path, for passing a constant to a BYREF parameter, and for assuming a BYVAL change reaches the caller.
syllabusPoints: Define and use a procedure, which may have none, one or more parameters.
Explain where in the construction of an algorithm it would be appropriate to use a procedure.
Use parameters, passed either by reference or by value.
Define and use a function; a function is used in an expression, and its return value replaces the call.
Explain where in the construction of an algorithm it is appropriate to use a function.
Use the terminology associated with procedures and functions, including procedure/function header, procedure/function interface, parameter, argument and return value.

definitions.definition: A named block of statements that carries out a task and is run with a CALL statement. It does not hand a value back to the point of call, although it can change the caller's variables through BYREF parameters.

A named block of statements that works out and returns exactly one value of a stated data type. It is called inside an expression, never with CALL, and the returned value takes the place of the call when the expression is evaluated.
The first line of a procedure or function definition: the keyword, the identifier, the parameter list with each parameter's data type (and BYVAL/BYREF), and for a function the RETURNS data type.
What the rest of the program needs to know to use a subroutine: the number, order, data types and passing method of its parameters, and for a function the type of value it returns.
An identifier listed in the subroutine header that acts as a variable inside the subroutine and receives a value (or, BYREF, access to a variable) when the subroutine is called.
The actual value, variable or expression written in the brackets of a call, matched by position to the corresponding parameter.
The single value a function sends back with RETURN; it replaces the function call in the expression that called it.
The parameter receives a copy of the argument's value, so changes made inside the subroutine do not affect the caller's variable. It is the default when no method is stated.

The parameter receives the address of the caller's variable, so the parameter and the argument are the same memory location and any change made inside the procedure is still there after the call. The argument must be a variable.

sections.title: Subroutines: giving a block of code a name
content: A subroutine is a set of statements that has been given an identifier so it can be run by name from anywhere in the program. Cambridge pseudocode has two kinds: procedures and functions. Both are written out once, above the main program that uses them, and are then run by calling them. When the subroutine finishes, control goes back to the statement just after the point of call.

Subroutines are how the modules found by decomposition (9.1) and drawn on a structure chart (12.2) turn into code. Because each one has a single job and receives its data through parameters, it can be written, tested and corrected on its own, and then used again wherever the same job is needed.
bullets: Two kinds of subroutine: a procedure (run with CALL) and a function (used inside an expression, returns one value).
Definitions come before the main program; a call jumps into the subroutine and control returns to the line after the call.
Data goes in through parameters; a function sends one value back with RETURN.

sections.title: Defining and calling a procedure
content: A procedure is written PROCEDURE <identifier>(<parameter list>), then its statements, then ENDPROCEDURE. The brackets may be empty, or hold one or more parameters, each written <identifier> : <data type> and separated by commas. The parameters behave as variables inside the procedure body. Any variable the procedure needs just for its own work is declared inside it, so it is local.

A procedure is run with CALL <identifier>(<arguments>), and this is a complete statement on its own line. The arguments must match the parameters in number, order and data type: the first argument goes to the first parameter, and so on. A procedure with no parameters is still called with empty brackets, CALL <identifier>(). Unless BYREF is written, parameters are passed by value.
bullets: Syntax: PROCEDURE Name(P1 : TYPE, P2 : TYPE) … ENDPROCEDURE; with no parameters, PROCEDURE Name() … ENDPROCEDURE.
Call: CALL Name(arg1, arg2) as a statement by itself; CALL Name() when there are no parameters.
Arguments are matched to parameters by position, so the order and data types must agree.
Variables declared inside the procedure are local to it.

examples.label: Procedures with no, one and two parameters
examples.content:
PROCEDURE ShowRule()
   OUTPUT "----------"
ENDPROCEDURE

PROCEDURE ShowTitle(Title : STRING)
   OUTPUT "== ", Title, " =="
ENDPROCEDURE

PROCEDURE ShowRow(Symbol : STRING, Count : INTEGER)
   DECLARE Line : STRING
   DECLARE Index : INTEGER
   Line ← ""
   FOR Index ← 1 TO Count
      Line ← Line & Symbol
   NEXT Index
   OUTPUT Line
ENDPROCEDURE

// main program
CALL ShowTitle("Pattern")
CALL ShowRule()
CALL ShowRow("*", 3)
CALL ShowRow("#", 5)
CALL ShowRule()

Output:
== Pattern ==
----------
***
#####
----------

ShowRow is called twice with different arguments: "*" and 3 the first time, "#" and 5 the second. Line and Index are local, so each call starts with its own fresh copies.

sections.title: Where a procedure is appropriate
content: Use a procedure when a part of the algorithm is an action rather than a calculation of one answer: displaying a menu or a report, writing records to a file, sorting an array, or reading and validating several inputs. It is also the right choice when a task has to change more than one of the caller's variables, since a procedure can do this through BYREF parameters, whereas a function returns only one value.

In practice a procedure is worth writing whenever the same group of steps appears in more than one place, or whenever a step of the design is big enough to be its own sub-task. Writing it once removes duplicated code, gives the main program a short, readable outline of calls, allows the procedure to be tested by itself, and means a later fix is made in one place only.
bullets: Choose a procedure for an action with no single result: output, file handling, updating an array, input with validation.
Choose a procedure (with BYREF parameters) when several of the caller's variables must be updated.
Any repeated group of steps is a candidate: write once, call many times, fix in one place.
Each procedure can be tested on its own before it is joined to the rest of the program.

sections.title: Defining and using a function
content: A function is written FUNCTION <identifier>(<parameter list>) RETURNS <data type>, then its statements, then ENDFUNCTION. The body must contain a RETURN <expression> statement on every path through it, and the value returned must be of the type named after RETURNS. RETURN takes effect at once: the function stops, and any statements after it are skipped. This allows a function to have more than one RETURN, for example one in each branch of an IF.

A function call is not a statement by itself, so it is never preceded by CALL. It is written where a value is needed: on the right of an assignment, in an OUTPUT list, in a condition, or as an argument to another call. When the function reaches RETURN, the returned value replaces the call and the rest of the expression is then evaluated. The pseudocode guide also says parameters should not be passed BYREF to a function, so a function's only effect on the caller is its return value.
bullets: Syntax: FUNCTION Name(P1 : TYPE) RETURNS TYPE … RETURN value … ENDFUNCTION.
Every path through the body must reach a RETURN; RETURN ends the function immediately.
Call it inside an expression, never with CALL; the return value replaces the call.
Function parameters are passed by value.

examples.label: Trace: return values replacing calls in expressions
examples.content:
FUNCTION Square(N : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
   RETURN N * N
ENDFUNCTION

FUNCTION Larger(A : INTEGER, B : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
   IF A > B THEN
      RETURN A
   ENDIF
   RETURN B
ENDFUNCTION

DECLARE Result : INTEGER
Result ← 50 + Square(3) * 2
OUTPUT Larger(Result, Square(8))
OUTPUT Larger(4, 7)

Step-by-step:
Result ← 50 + Square(3) * 2
   Square(3) returns 9     → 50 + 9 * 2
   * before +              → 50 + 18 = 68, so Result = 68
OUTPUT Larger(Result, Square(8))
   Square(8) returns 64    → Larger(68, 64)
   68 > 64 is TRUE         → RETURN 68; the final RETURN B is never reached
   Output: 68
OUTPUT Larger(4, 7)
   4 > 7 is FALSE          → skip the IF, reach RETURN 7
   Output: 7

Writing CALL Square(3) would be wrong: the 9 it returns would have nowhere to go.

sections.title: Where a function is appropriate: procedure or function?
content: Use a function when a part of the algorithm works out one answer that the caller then uses: a total, an average, the larger of two values, the position of an item in an array, or a TRUE/FALSE result from a validation check such as IsValidDate(Day, Month, Year). Because the answer comes back as a value, it can go straight into an expression or a condition, for example IF IsValidDate(D, M, Y) THEN … . The built-in routines such as LENGTH, MID and INT are functions for exactly this reason.

The quick test is to ask what the caller needs back. If the answer is one value, write a function. If the answer is nothing, or several values, write a procedure (using BYREF for values that must come back). Converting one into the other changes the call as well as the header: a procedure call is a CALL statement, while a function call sits inside an expression.
bullets: Function: exactly one value is needed back, often used in a calculation or condition.
Procedure: an action with no value back, or several values back through BYREF.
Validation checks are often written as BOOLEAN functions so they can be used directly in IF or WHILE conditions.

sections.title: Local and global variables
content: A variable declared inside a procedure or function is local: it exists only while that call is running and cannot be seen from the main program or from other subroutines. Parameters behave the same way. Each new call creates fresh local variables, so no value is carried over from a previous call. A variable declared in the main program, outside every subroutine, is global and can be read or changed from anywhere.

Good practice is to keep any variable that a subroutine alone needs as a local, and to pass data in through parameters rather than relying on globals. A subroutine that quietly reads or alters a global is harder to reuse and to test, because its behaviour depends on something not shown in its header. Exam questions sometimes state that an array is global to keep the answer short; otherwise, use parameters.
bullets: Local: declared inside a subroutine, exists only during that call, invisible outside it.
Global: declared outside all subroutines, visible everywhere.
Prefer locals and parameters; hidden use of globals makes subroutines harder to test and reuse.

sections.title: Terminology: header, interface, parameter, argument, return value
content: The header is the first line of a definition. It names the subroutine and lists its parameters with their data types, and for a function it ends with RETURNS and a type. A parameter is one of the identifiers in that list; inside the body it is used like a variable. An argument is what is actually supplied in the brackets when the subroutine is called; it can be a literal, a variable or a whole expression (except that a BYREF argument must be a variable). Arguments are matched to parameters by position, not by name, so the names do not need to agree.

The interface is everything a programmer needs to know to use the subroutine without reading its body: how many parameters there are, their order, data types and passing method, and the type of value a function returns. The return value is the single value that a function's RETURN statement sends back. Because callers depend only on the interface, the body can later be rewritten, for instance to make it faster, without changing a single call.
bullets: Header: the first line, with identifier, parameter list and (for a function) RETURNS type.
Parameter: an identifier in the header. Argument: the value or variable given in the call.
Interface: number, order, types and passing method of the parameters, plus the return type.
Return value: the one value sent back by RETURN, which replaces the function call.

examples.label: Labelling the parts of a function and its calls
examples.content:
FUNCTION CountChar(Word : STRING, Target : STRING) RETURNS INTEGER   // header
   DECLARE Index, Total : INTEGER                                   // local variables
   Total ← 0
   FOR Index ← 1 TO LENGTH(Word)
      IF MID(Word, Index, 1) = Target THEN
         Total ← Total + 1
      ENDIF
   NEXT Index
   RETURN Total                                                     // return value
ENDFUNCTION

DECLARE Place : STRING
DECLARE Count : INTEGER
Place ← "Mississippi"
Count ← CountChar("banana", "a") + CountChar(Place, "s")

Parameters:  Word, Target
Arguments:   "banana" and "a" in the first call; Place and "s" in the second
Interface:   two STRING parameters (by value, the default), returns an INTEGER
Trace:       CountChar("banana", "a") returns 3 (positions 2, 4, 6)
             CountChar("Mississippi", "s") returns 4 (positions 3, 4, 6, 7)
             Count ← 3 + 4, so Count = 7

sections.title: Passing parameters BYVAL and BYREF
content: Writing BYVAL or BYREF in front of a parameter in the header states how it is passed. BYVAL copies the argument's current value into the parameter; the procedure works on that copy, and the caller's variable is exactly as it was when the call ends. The argument may therefore be a literal or an expression. BYREF passes the address of the caller's variable, so inside the procedure the parameter is just another name for that same memory location. Every assignment to the parameter changes the caller's variable, and the argument must be a variable, not a constant or an expression.

If neither keyword is written, BYVAL is assumed. A keyword also carries on to the parameters that follow it until the other keyword appears, so in PROCEDURE Swap(BYREF X : INTEGER, Y : INTEGER) both X and Y are passed by reference. BYREF is used with procedures only; functions take BYVAL parameters and send their result back with RETURN. Choose BYREF when the purpose of the procedure is to update the caller's variables, and BYVAL whenever the caller's data should be protected.
bullets: BYVAL: a copy is passed; the caller's variable cannot be changed; argument may be any expression. Default.
BYREF: the variable's address is passed; changes inside the procedure remain after the call; argument must be a variable.
A BYVAL/BYREF keyword applies to the following parameters too, until the other keyword is written.
Do not use BYREF with a function: a function returns its result with RETURN.

sections.title: Worked traces: BYVAL and BYREF side by side
content: To decide what a call does to the caller, trace the caller's variables before and after each call, not just the parameters. In the first trace, Step is BYVAL and Total is BYREF. Doubling Step changes only the copy, so P stays 3 however many times the procedure is called, while every change to Total is made directly to Q.

The second trace uses the same swap body twice. With BYREF applying to both parameters, the values are exchanged. With Y marked BYVAL, the assignment Y ← Temp changes only a copy, so the caller ends with the same value in both variables. That half-working swap is a classic exam trace.
bullets: Always record the caller's variables after the call returns: that is where BYVAL and BYREF differ.
A BYVAL parameter can be changed inside the procedure; the change is simply thrown away at the end.
A swap needs both parameters BYREF; with one BYVAL, both variables end up holding the same value.

examples.label: Trace 1: one BYVAL and one BYREF parameter, called twice
examples.content:
PROCEDURE Update(BYVAL Step : INTEGER, BYREF Total : INTEGER)
   Step ← Step * 2
   Total ← Total + Step
ENDPROCEDURE

DECLARE P, Q : INTEGER
P ← 3
Q ← 4
CALL Update(P, Q)
OUTPUT P, " ", Q
CALL Update(P, Q)
OUTPUT P, " ", Q

Statement             | Step | Total (= Q) | P | Q  | OUTPUT
P ← 3, Q ← 4          |      |             | 3 | 4  |
CALL Update: enter    | 3    | 4           | 3 | 4  |
Step ← Step * 2       | 6    | 4           | 3 | 4  |
Total ← Total + Step  | 6    | 10          | 3 | 10 |
return, OUTPUT        |      |             | 3 | 10 | 3 10
CALL Update: enter    | 3    | 10          | 3 | 10 |
Step ← Step * 2       | 6    | 10          | 3 | 10 |
Total ← Total + Step  | 6    | 16          | 3 | 16 |
return, OUTPUT        |      |             | 3 | 16 | 3 16

Step starts at 3 on each call because it is a fresh copy of P; Q keeps growing because Total is Q.

examples.label: Trace 2: a swap with both parameters BYREF, then with Y BYVAL
examples.content:
PROCEDURE SwapBoth(BYREF X : INTEGER, Y : INTEGER)     // BYREF covers X and Y
   DECLARE Temp : INTEGER
   Temp ← X
   X ← Y
   Y ← Temp
ENDPROCEDURE

PROCEDURE SwapOne(BYREF X : INTEGER, BYVAL Y : INTEGER) // only X is BYREF
   DECLARE Temp : INTEGER
   Temp ← X
   X ← Y
   Y ← Temp
ENDPROCEDURE

First ← 1
Second ← 2
CALL SwapBoth(First, Second)
   Temp ← 1; X ← 2 (First = 2); Y ← 1 (Second = 1)
   After the call: First = 2, Second = 1   → swapped

First ← 1
Second ← 2
CALL SwapOne(First, Second)
   Temp ← 1; X ← 2 (First = 2); Y ← 1 changes only the copy
   After the call: First = 2, Second = 2   → not swapped

examples.label: Python check of both traces (BYREF simulated with a one-item list)
examples.content:
# Assigning to an int parameter in Python never changes the caller's
# variable, so it behaves like BYVAL. To imitate BYREF, pass a one-item
# list and change item [0], which the caller can see.

def update(step, total_ref):        # BYVAL Step, BYREF Total
    step = step * 2
    total_ref[0] = total_ref[0] + step

p, q = 3, [4]
update(p, q)
print(p, q[0])                      # 3 10
update(p, q)
print(p, q[0])                      # 3 16

def swap_one(x_ref, y):              # BYREF X, BYVAL Y
    temp = x_ref[0]
    x_ref[0] = y
    y = temp                         # only the local copy changes

first, second = [1], 2
swap_one(first, second)
print(first[0], second)             # 2 2

sections.title: Writing efficient pseudocode
content: Efficient pseudocode reaches the correct result without doing unnecessary work. Three habits cover most exam questions. First, do not repeat a calculation whose answer does not change: work it out once before a loop, or store a function's return value in a variable instead of calling the function twice. Second, stop a loop as soon as the answer is known: a search that has found its item should not keep checking the rest of the array, so a WHILE or REPEAT loop with a flag suits it better than a FOR loop over every element. Third, reuse modules: one procedure with parameters is better than several near-identical copies.

Choosing the right structure is part of efficiency as well: a CASE instead of a long chain of separate IFs that are all tested, a FOR loop when the number of passes is fixed, and a condition-controlled loop when it is not. Efficient code is also usually shorter and clearer, which reduces the chance of errors.
bullets: Move calculations that do not change out of the loop; store a return value rather than calling the same function again.
Exit early: use a condition-controlled loop with a flag when the job can finish before the end of the data.
Reuse one parameterised subroutine rather than writing several similar ones.
Use IF … ELSE or CASE so that once one branch is chosen the other tests are skipped.

examples.label: Worked example: removing wasted work
examples.content:
// 1. Repeated calculation
// Wasteful: Average(Marks) is worked out twice
IF Average(Marks) >= 50 THEN
   OUTPUT "Pass, mean ", Average(Marks)
ENDIF
// Better: call once, keep the return value
Mean ← Average(Marks)
IF Mean >= 50 THEN
   OUTPUT "Pass, mean ", Mean
ENDIF

// 2. Exiting a loop early (Names has 1000 elements, SearchName is in Names[3])
// Wasteful: always checks all 1000 elements
Found ← FALSE
FOR Index ← 1 TO 1000
   IF Names[Index] = SearchName THEN
      Found ← TRUE
   ENDIF
NEXT Index
// Better: stops as soon as the name is found
Found ← FALSE
Index ← 1
WHILE Index <= 1000 AND NOT Found
   IF Names[Index] = SearchName THEN
      Found ← TRUE
   ELSE
      Index ← Index + 1
   ENDIF
ENDWHILE

Comparisons of Names[Index] with SearchName:
   FOR version:   1000 (every element)
   WHILE version: 3 (Index 1 no, 2 no, 3 yes; Found = TRUE ends the loop, Index = 3)

comparisonTable.title: Procedure versus function in Cambridge pseudocode
rows: CALL Name(args) as a statement on its own
Inside an expression, e.g. X ← Name(args); never with CALL
None directly; the caller's variables can be changed through BYREF
Exactly one value, by RETURN, which replaces the call
Actions: output, file handling, updating arrays or several variables
Working out one result: a calculation, a search position, a TRUE/FALSE check

diagram.title: What happens when a subroutine is called
nodes: Call reached: CALL Name(args) for a procedure, or Name(args) inside an expression for a function
Arguments matched to parameters by position: BYVAL copies the value, BYREF passes the variable's address
Local variables created; the body runs
Procedure: reaches ENDPROCEDURE. Function: reaches RETURN, which ends it at once
Local variables and BYVAL copies discarded; BYREF changes stay in the caller's variables
Control returns: after the CALL line, or the return value replaces the call and the expression is finished

analysisChains.title: A 'reset' procedure that does not reset
steps: PROCEDURE Reset(Total : INTEGER) sets Total ← 0, and the main program runs CALL Reset(RunningTotal) with RunningTotal = 50
No passing method is written, so BYVAL is assumed and Total receives a copy of 50
Total ← 0 changes the copy only; the copy is discarded at ENDPROCEDURE
After the call RunningTotal is still 50
analysisChains.evaluation: The header must be PROCEDURE Reset(BYREF Total : INTEGER) so that Total refers to RunningTotal itself. Alternatively, drop the procedure and write RunningTotal ← 0 directly; a subroutine is not worth it for one assignment.

analysisChains.title: Choosing between a procedure and a function for a validation step
steps: A program must check a date entered as Day, Month and Year before storing it, in several different places
The check produces a single answer, valid or not, which each caller uses to decide what to do next
Written as FUNCTION IsValidDate(Day : INTEGER, Month : INTEGER, Year : INTEGER) RETURNS BOOLEAN, it can be used directly as IF IsValidDate(D, M, Y) THEN or in a REPEAT … UNTIL condition
As a procedure it would need an extra BYREF BOOLEAN parameter and a separate CALL line before every test
analysisChains.evaluation: A function is the better choice: exactly one value comes back, it fits straight into the conditions that need it, and there is no BYREF side effect. Because the check is needed in several places, making it a subroutine at all also removes duplicated code.

analysisChains.title: Making a search loop efficient
steps: A FOR loop compares SearchName with all 1000 elements of Names and sets Found ← TRUE on a match
When the name is at position 3, the remaining 997 comparisons cannot change the result
Replacing it with WHILE Index <= 1000 AND NOT Found, incrementing Index only when there is no match, stops after 3 comparisons
When the name is absent both versions make 1000 comparisons, and the WHILE version must still not read beyond Names[1000]
analysisChains.evaluation: The early-exit loop is never slower and is usually much faster, and it leaves Index holding the position found. The upper-bound test must stay in the WHILE condition, or a missing name makes the loop run past the end of the array.

examTips: Write the header in full: PROCEDURE Name(BYREF X : INTEGER) or FUNCTION Name(X : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER. A missing data type or missing RETURNS type costs the header mark.
Use CALL only for procedures. A function goes inside an expression: an assignment, an OUTPUT or a condition.
In a trace, write down the caller's variables after every call; BYVAL leaves them unchanged, BYREF does not.
When asked where a procedure or function is appropriate, link it to the task: one value back → function; an action or several values back → procedure; repeated steps → subroutine.
For 'write efficient pseudocode', name what you avoided: a repeated calculation, an unneeded pass through a loop, or duplicated code.
commonMistakes: Writing CALL in front of a function, or using a procedure call inside an expression as if it returned a value.
Leaving a path through a function with no RETURN, or forgetting that statements after RETURN are never run.
Assuming a change to a BYVAL parameter (including an unmarked one, since BYVAL is the default) is seen by the caller.
Reading PROCEDURE Swap(BYREF X : INTEGER, Y : INTEGER) as if only X were BYREF; the keyword carries on to Y.
Passing a literal or an expression, such as CALL Update(3, Q + 1), to a BYREF parameter; a BYREF argument must be a variable.
Mixing up parameter (in the header) and argument (in the call), or expecting their names to match.

quickRecall.question: How is a procedure with no parameters defined and called?
quickRecall.answer: PROCEDURE Name() … ENDPROCEDURE, called with the statement CALL Name().

quickRecall.question: Give the general form of a function header.
quickRecall.answer: FUNCTION Name(P1 : TYPE, P2 : TYPE) RETURNS TYPE.

quickRecall.question: What happens to a function call when RETURN is executed?
quickRecall.answer: The function ends immediately and the returned value replaces the call in the expression, which is then evaluated.

quickRecall.question: What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?
quickRecall.answer: A parameter is the identifier listed in the subroutine header; an argument is the actual value, variable or expression supplied in the call.

quickRecall.question: What does a subroutine's interface consist of?
quickRecall.answer: The number, order, data types and passing method of its parameters, and for a function the data type returned.

quickRecall.question: After PROCEDURE Update(BYVAL Step : INTEGER, BYREF Total : INTEGER) with Step ← Step * 2 and Total ← Total + Step, what are P and Q after CALL Update(P, Q) with P = 3, Q = 4?
quickRecall.answer: P = 3 (only a copy was doubled) and Q = 10 (4 + 6, changed through BYREF).

quickRecall.question: If no BYVAL or BYREF is written, how is a parameter passed?
quickRecall.answer: By value; BYVAL is the default.

quickRecall.question: When is a function more appropriate than a procedure?
quickRecall.answer: When the task produces exactly one value that the caller uses, for example in a calculation or as a condition.
